column9: stem
column28: explanation

column9: Which pair of elements would bond to form a covalent compound?
column28: Sulfur and oxygen are both nonmetals, and two nonmetals make a covalent compound. Each of the other pairs has a metal (Na, Ca, K) with a nonmetal, which makes an ionic compound.
column29: Find the pair where BOTH elements are right of the staircase on the periodic table.

column9: When two nonmetals bond together, they form a(n) ___ compound.
column28: Two nonmetals make a covalent compound. Metal + nonmetal makes an ionic compound.
column29: Which type of bond involves sharing electrons?

column9: Where are the metals found on the periodic table?
column14: To the right of the staircase line
column15: To the left of the staircase line
column28: Metals sit left of the staircase on the periodic table. Nonmetals are to the right, and Group 18 holds the noble gases.
column29: Sodium and calcium are metals. Which side of the table are they on?

column9: A covalent bond forms between a metal and a nonmetal.
column28: False. Metal + nonmetal makes an ionic bond. A covalent bond forms between nonmetals.
column29: Which type of compound does the metal + nonmetal rule give?

column9: When potassium and fluorine bond, electrons are transferred rather than shared.
column28: True. Potassium is a metal and fluorine is a nonmetal, so they form an ionic bond: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal.
column29: Is potassium a metal or a nonmetal? Is fluorine?

column9: In a covalent bond, the atoms ___ electrons.
column28: Covalent bonds form between nonmetals that share electrons. In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred instead.
column29: Ionic bonds transfer electrons. Covalent bonds do something different with them.

column9: Match each bonding term to its meaning.
column14: Ionic bond :: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal
column15: Covalent bond :: Nonmetal atoms share electrons
column16: Molecule :: A compound formed when elements are covalently bonded
column17: Octet rule :: Atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons
column28: Ionic = transfer from a metal to a nonmetal. Covalent = sharing between nonmetals. A molecule is made of covalently bonded atoms. The octet rule says most atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons.
column29: Start with the two bond types: which one moves electrons, and which one shares them?

column9: Which of these elements is a metal?
column28: Potassium (Group 1) is left of the staircase, so it is a metal. Sulfur, chlorine, and nitrogen are all right of the staircase, so they are nonmetals.
column29: Find each element on the periodic table. Which one is left of the staircase?

column9: Which compound is ionic?
column28: KCl has a metal (potassium) and a nonmetal (chlorine), so it is ionic. CH₄, H₂O, and SO₂ are made only of nonmetals, so they are covalent.
column29: Look for the one compound that contains a metal.

column9: How many electrons are shared in one single covalent bond?
column28: A single bond shares 2 electrons (one pair). A double bond shares 4 and a triple bond shares 6.
column29: A single bond is one shared pair of electrons.

column9: Covalent compounds can be solids, liquids, or gases at room temperature.
column28: True. Covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points, so they can be solids (sugar), liquids (ethanol), or gases (carbon dioxide). Ionic compounds are usually solid crystals.
column29: Think of sugar, rubbing alcohol, and carbon dioxide. Are they all the same state?

column9: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
column17: To lose all of their electrons
column28: Atoms bond to be stable, usually by getting 8 electrons in their outer shell. Bonding does not change which element an atom is.
column29: Think about the octet rule. What do atoms get when their outer shell is full?

column9: By the octet rule, most atoms are stable when they have ___ electrons in their outer shell.
column28: Octet means 8. Most elements are stable with 8 outer electrons; hydrogen and helium are the exceptions.
column29: Noble gases like neon already have this many outer electrons.

column9: Which property is typical of an ionic compound?
column14: Low melting point; often a liquid or gas
column15: High melting point and forms crystals
column16: Does not conduct electricity when dissolved
column28: Ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C and form crystals. The other choices describe covalent compounds.
column29: Ionic bonds are strong. Does that make the compound easy or hard to melt?

column9: Select every element that is a nonmetal. Select all that apply.
column28: Oxygen, chlorine, and nitrogen are right of the staircase, so they are nonmetals. Sodium, magnesium, and calcium are in Groups 1 and 2, left of the staircase, so they are metals.
column29: Check each element's spot on the periodic table: left of the staircase is metal, right is nonmetal.

column9: Select every compound that is ionic. Select all that apply.
column28: LiF, K₂O, and SrO each have a metal (Li, K, Sr) bonded to a nonmetal, so they are ionic. CO₂, N₂O₄, and SO₂ are only nonmetals, so they are covalent.
column29: For each formula, ask: is the first element a metal (left of the staircase)?

column9: Which pair of atoms will form an ionic bond?
column28: Barium is a metal and bromine is a nonmetal, so they form an ionic bond. N and O and S and F are two nonmetals (covalent). K and Na are both metals, so they do not form an ionic compound.
column29: An ionic bond needs exactly one metal and one nonmetal.

column9: Which formula represents a substance that contains covalent bonds?
column28: Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals, so PCl₃ has covalent bonds. CaO, Li₂S, and BaF₂ each start with a metal, so they are ionic.
column29: Covalent bonds form between nonmetals. Which formula has no metal in it?

column9: NH₄Cl contains the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. How should NH₄Cl be classified?
column14: Ionic, because it contains the polyatomic ion ammonium
column15: Covalent, because every element in it is a nonmetal
column16: Ionic, because nitrogen is a metal
column17: Covalent, because it has more than two elements
column28: A compound with a polyatomic ion is ionic, and that includes ammonium compounds like NH₄Cl. The NH₄⁺ ion acts like a metal ion and bonds to Cl⁻. Using only the nonmetal rule is the common mistake here.
column29: What is the rule for compounds that contain a polyatomic ion?

column9: Sodium sulfate is Na₂SO₄ (sulfate is SO₄²⁻). Which classification and reason are correct?
column14: Covalent, because sulfur and oxygen are both nonmetals
column15: Ionic, because the metal sodium is bonded to the sulfate ion
column16: Covalent, because it contains more than two elements
column17: Ionic, because sulfate contains a metal
column28: Sodium is a metal bonded to the polyatomic ion sulfate, so Na₂SO₄ is ionic. The S and O inside sulfate are held together by sharing, but the compound as a whole is classified as ionic. Sulfate has no metal in it.
column29: Look at the first element. Is it a metal? Then look for a polyatomic ion.

column9: Magnesium and oxygen bond to form a compound. What happens to the electrons?
column17: No electrons move; the atoms just stick
column28: Mg is a metal and O is a nonmetal, so the bond is ionic: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal. Sharing happens only between nonmetals.
column29: Is this metal + nonmetal or nonmetal + nonmetal? Then: which one gives electrons away?

column9: Hydrogen is on the left side of the periodic table, so it counts as a metal when you classify a compound.
column28: False. Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits above Group 1. A compound like H₂O is two nonmetals, so it is covalent.
column29: Is hydrogen a shiny solid like sodium, or a gas like nitrogen?

column9: CuCl₂ is ionic, even though copper is a transition metal and not in Group 1 or 2.
column28: True. Copper is left of the staircase, so it is a metal. Any metal bonded to a nonmetal makes an ionic compound, including transition metals like copper and iron.
column29: Is copper left or right of the staircase?

column9: Nitrogen gas, N₂, has a triple bond between its two atoms. How many electrons are shared in a triple bond?
column28: Each bond shares one pair (2 electrons), so a triple bond shares 3 × 2 = 6 electrons.
column29: A single bond shares 2 electrons. A triple bond is three bonds.

column9: Carbon dioxide has two double bonds: O=C=O. How many electrons are shared in total in one CO₂ molecule?
column28: Each double bond shares 4 electrons, so 2 × 4 = 8 shared electrons. A common mistake is counting only the 2 bonds or only one pair per bond.
column29: Find how many electrons one double bond shares, then count the double bonds.

column9: Match each compound to the reason for its classification.
column14: LiCl :: Group 1 metal + nonmetal, so ionic
column16: Ca(NO₃)₂ (nitrate is NO₃⁻) :: Metal + polyatomic ion, so ionic
column17: NH₄Br (ammonium is NH₄⁺) :: Only nonmetal atoms, but ammonium makes it ionic
column18: Cu₂O :: Transition metal + nonmetal, so ionic
column28: LiCl: metal + nonmetal. N₂O: two nonmetals. Ca(NO₃)₂: metal + polyatomic ion. NH₄Br: ammonium is a polyatomic ion, so it is ionic even with no metal. Cu₂O: copper is a transition metal, still a metal.
column29: For each formula, check for a metal, then check for a polyatomic ion.

column9: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is made only of nonmetal atoms that share electrons. One unit of a covalent compound like this is called a ___.
column28: A molecule is a compound formed when 2 or more elements are covalently bonded. Ethanol is all nonmetals sharing electrons, so its units are molecules.
column29: What is the vocabulary word for a covalently bonded unit?

column9: Maya dissolves an unknown white solid in water. The solution lights up the conductivity tester. What does this suggest about the solid?
column14: It is covalent, because only covalent compounds dissolve in water
column15: It is covalent, because it is a white solid
column16: It is ionic, because every compound that dissolves is ionic
column17: It is ionic, because it breaks into free-moving ions in water
column28: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved because they break into free-moving ions that carry the current. Dissolving by itself proves nothing (sugar dissolves too), and color is irrelevant.
column29: What has to be moving around in the water for electricity to flow?

column9: Jae dissolves sugar in water and tests it. The bulb does not light. Why doesn't the sugar solution conduct electricity?
column14: Sugar stays as whole molecules, so there are no ions to carry current
column15: Sugar is ionic, but its ions are too large to move
column16: Sugar does not actually dissolve in water
column17: The water blocks electricity from reaching the sugar
column28: Sugar is covalent. When it dissolves, it stays as whole molecules, so there are no charged ions to carry current. Ionic compounds like KI break into free-moving ions and do conduct.
column29: Is sugar made of metals and nonmetals, or only nonmetals? What does that mean for ions?

column9: Potassium bromide, KBr, is made of a metal and a nonmetal. Select every property you would expect it to have. Select all that apply.
column15: Conducts electricity when dissolved in water
column28: KBr is ionic, so it has a high melting point, forms crystals, and conducts when dissolved. Ionic compounds transfer electrons rather than share, and they are usually solids, not gases.
column29: First decide ionic or covalent, then recall that type's properties.

column9: Select every compound that is covalent. Select all that apply.
column28: CCl₄, NO₂, and PF₃ contain only nonmetals, so they are covalent. CaS, CuO, and Li₂O each have a metal (Ca, Cu, Li), so they are ionic. Copper is a transition metal but still a metal.
column29: Covalent means no metal at all. Check the first element of each formula.

column9: Aluminum oxide is Al₂O₃. Which classification and reason are correct?
column14: Covalent, because aluminum is in Group 13, not Group 1 or 2
column15: Ionic, because aluminum is left of the staircase (a metal) and oxygen is a nonmetal
column16: Covalent, because it has more oxygen atoms than aluminum atoms
column17: Ionic, because oxygen is a metal
column28: Aluminum is a metal (left of the staircase) and oxygen is a nonmetal, so Al₂O₃ is ionic. The number of atoms does not decide bond type, and metals are not only in Groups 1 and 2.
column29: Find aluminum on the periodic table. Which side of the staircase is it on?

column9: Hydrogen needs the same number of outer electrons as oxygen to be stable.
column28: False. Most elements, like oxygen, are stable with 8 outer electrons, but hydrogen (and helium) are the exceptions: hydrogen is stable with 2.
column29: The octet rule has two exceptions. Which elements are they?

column9: Group B wants to know if a white solid is ionic or covalent. Which measurement is the most useful evidence?
column17: Which shelf it was stored on
column28: Melting point is relevant: ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C, covalent ones much lower. Color, mass, and storage location do not depend on the bond type.
column29: Which choice is a property that changes depending on how strong the bonds are?

column9: Leo says calcium and magnesium will form an ionic compound because they are both metals. Which response is best?
column14: Leo is right: two metals always form an ionic bond
column15: Leo is wrong: they form a covalent bond because they are in the same group
column16: Leo is right: calcium transfers electrons to magnesium
column17: Leo is wrong: ionic compounds need a metal and a nonmetal, and both of these are metals
column28: An ionic compound forms between a metal and a nonmetal. Calcium and magnesium are both metals, so they do not form an ionic compound, and covalent bonds are between nonmetals, not metals.
column29: Restate the ionic rule. Does Ca + Mg fit it?

column9: Lab data — A: melts at 801 °C, white, solution conducts. B: melts at −95 °C, colorless, solution does not conduct. C: melts at 186 °C, white, solution does not conduct. D: melts at 680 °C, white, solution conducts. Select every substance that is most likely ionic. Select all that apply.
column28: A and D melt well above 300 °C and conduct when dissolved, so they are ionic. B and C melt far below 300 °C and do not conduct, so they are covalent. Color is the same for A, C, and D, so it cannot separate them.
column29: Use the two properties that depend on bond type: melting point (about 300 °C) and conductivity when dissolved.

column9: Substance C melts at 186 °C and its solution does not conduct, but it forms white crystals. Lena says the crystals prove C is ionic. Which response is best?
column14: Lena is wrong: the low melting point and no conductivity show C is covalent; covalent compounds can be solid crystals too
column15: Lena is right: only ionic compounds form crystals, so C must be ionic
column16: Lena is right: 186 °C is a high temperature, so C is ionic
column17: Lena is wrong: C is covalent because it is white
column28: Crystals alone do not decide the bond type, since covalent solids like sugar form crystals too. C melts below 300 °C and does not conduct when dissolved, so it is covalent. Color is irrelevant evidence.
column29: Which two pieces of evidence actually depend on bond type? What do they say for C?

column9: Jae records three things about each unknown: melting point, color, and whether its solution conducts. Which of these could NOT help him classify the unknowns as ionic or covalent?
column28: Color does not depend on bond type: both ionic and covalent compounds can be white or colorless. Melting point (above or below about 300 °C) and conductivity when dissolved are relevant evidence.
column29: Ask of each one: does it depend on whether electrons were transferred or shared?

column9: A student says, "Water must be ionic, because salt dissolves in it." Water melts at 0 °C. Which is the best evaluation of the claim?
column14: Correct: anything that can dissolve salt must be ionic
column15: Correct: water and salt are found together in the ocean, so they are the same type
column16: Wrong: water is made of two nonmetals and melts far below 300 °C, so it is covalent; dissolving salt says nothing about water's bonds
column17: Wrong: water is a liquid, and liquids can never be ionic
column28: Water (H₂O) is hydrogen and oxygen, two nonmetals, and its 0 °C melting point is far below 300 °C, so it is covalent. What water can dissolve is irrelevant evidence. Saying liquids can never be ionic reaches the right answer for a wrong reason.
column29: Ignore the salt. What are water's own elements, and what does its melting point tell you?

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺, nitrate is NO₃⁻, and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Select every compound that is ionic. Select all that apply.
column28: NH₄NO₃ is two polyatomic ions (ammonium and nitrate), so it is ionic even with no metal. Fe₂O₃ and PbCl₂ have metals (iron, lead). CaCO₃ is calcium with carbonate. N₂O₅ and CS₂ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, so they are covalent.
column29: Check each formula for a metal OR a polyatomic ion. Either one makes it ionic.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, ammonium is NH₄⁺, and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. How many of these six compounds are ionic? K₃PO₄, SF₆, NiCl₂, (NH₄)₂CO₃, P₂O₅, CO
column28: Ionic: K₃PO₄ (metal + phosphate), NiCl₂ (transition metal + nonmetal), and (NH₄)₂CO₃ (ammonium + carbonate) = 3. SF₆, P₂O₅, and CO are only nonmetals, so they are covalent.
column29: Sort each one: does it have a metal or a polyatomic ion? Count only those.

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻, ammonium is NH₄⁺, and hydroxide is OH⁻. Which list contains ONLY ionic compounds?
column28: NaC₂H₃O₂ (metal + acetate), CuO (copper is a metal), and NH₄I (ammonium) are all ionic. Each other list hides one covalent compound: CH₄, N₂O, or CO₂.
column29: In each list, hunt for a compound with no metal and no polyatomic ion.

column9: Priya tests an unknown that forms white crystals and melts at 45 °C. She says it must be ionic because it is a crystal solid. Which is the best evaluation?
column14: Wrong: 45 °C is far below 300 °C, so it is likely covalent; covalent compounds can be solids
column15: Right: every solid is an ionic compound
column16: Right: crystals always mean electrons were transferred
column17: Wrong: she has to know its mass before she can decide
column28: Ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C. A 45 °C melting point points to covalent, and covalent compounds can be solids. Mass is irrelevant evidence.
column29: Compare the melting point to the 300 °C guideline before you look at anything else.

column9: Which pair of observations makes the strongest case that an unknown compound is covalent?
column15: Melts at 95 °C; its solution does not conduct
column16: Forms white crystals; dissolves in water
column17: Has a mass of 25 g; its solution does not conduct
column28: Both observations in the key point to covalent: a low melting point and no free ions in solution. Crystals, dissolving, and mass do not show bond type, and the 1,200 °C conducting sample is ionic.
column29: You want BOTH observations to be relevant evidence, and both pointing the same way.

column9: (NH₄)₂SO₄ (ammonium is NH₄⁺, sulfate is SO₄²⁻) is made only of nonmetal atoms, so it must be covalent.
column28: False. It is made of two polyatomic ions, ammonium and sulfate, so it is ionic. Ammonium acts like the metal ion. The nonmetal rule does not apply when polyatomic ions are present.
column29: Which rule comes first: the nonmetal rule, or the polyatomic ion rule?

column9: Acetylene, C₂H₂, is drawn H–C≡C–H: two single bonds and one triple bond. How many electrons are shared in total in one acetylene molecule?
column28: Two single bonds share 2 × 2 = 4 electrons and the triple bond shares 6, so 4 + 6 = 10 shared electrons.
column29: Find the electrons for each bond type, then add them up for every bond in the drawing.

column9: A group tests an unknown. Match each observation to what it tells them about ionic vs covalent.
column15: Its solution does not light the bulb :: Points to covalent
column16: The sample is bright blue :: Irrelevant: color does not show bond type
column17: The sample has a mass of 12 g :: Irrelevant: mass depends on how much you have
column28: A melting point above 300 °C points to ionic. No conductivity when dissolved points to covalent (no free ions). Color and mass do not depend on how electrons are bonded, so they are irrelevant.
column29: Sort the evidence first: which observations depend on bond type and which don't?

column9: Which statement correctly compares the bonds in MgCl₂ and in chlorine gas, Cl₂?
column14: In both, the atoms share electrons, because chlorine is in both
column15: In MgCl₂, magnesium shares electrons with chlorine; in Cl₂, one chlorine transfers an electron to the other
column16: In MgCl₂, magnesium transfers electrons to chlorine; in Cl₂, the two chlorine atoms share electrons
column17: In both, electrons are transferred, because chlorine always forms ions
column28: MgCl₂ is metal + nonmetal, so the metal transfers electrons (ionic). Cl₂ is two identical nonmetal atoms, so they share electrons (covalent). The same element can be in both kinds of bond.
column29: Classify each one separately: is there a metal in it?

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Select every compound that is covalent. Select all that apply.
column28: N₂O₃, SCl₂, and PBr₅ are only nonmetals, so they are covalent. SnO₂, Cr₂O₃, and Co(NO₃)₂ have metals (tin, chromium, cobalt), so they are ionic, even though tin, chromium, and cobalt are not in Groups 1 or 2.
column29: Covalent means no metal and no polyatomic ion. Check whether Sn, Cr, and Co are left of the staircase.

column9: Dev says neon does not form compounds because it is a gas. Rae says neon does not form compounds because its outer shell is already full. Who has the stronger argument?
column14: Dev, because gases never form bonds
column15: Both, because every gas has a full outer shell
column16: Neither, because neon bonds easily with metals
column17: Rae, because a full outer shell means neon is already stable
column28: Atoms bond to become stable. Neon is a noble gas whose outer shell is already full, so it has no reason to bond. Dev's reason fails: oxygen and carbon dioxide are gases that have bonds.
column29: Why do atoms bond in the first place? Does neon need to?

column9: Which compound is made only of nonmetals, so it is covalent?
column28: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so CO is covalent. NaBr, MgS, and LiCl each start with a metal (Na, Mg, Li), so they are ionic.
column29: Look for the formula with no metal in it. Metals sit left of the staircase.

column9: Lithium and oxygen bond to make Li₂O. What type of compound is Li₂O?
column14: Ionic, because lithium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal
column15: Covalent, because lithium and oxygen are both nonmetals
column16: Covalent, because it has two lithium atoms
column17: Neither, because lithium and oxygen cannot bond
column28: Lithium (Group 1) is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so Li₂O is ionic. The number of atoms does not decide the bond type.
column29: Is lithium left or right of the staircase? Is oxygen?

column9: Phosphorus and fluorine bond to make PF₅. What type of compound is PF₅?
column14: Ionic, because phosphorus is a metal
column15: Ionic, because it has more than two atoms
column16: Covalent, because phosphorus and fluorine are both nonmetals
column17: Neither, because two nonmetals cannot bond
column28: Phosphorus and fluorine are both right of the staircase, so they are nonmetals. Two nonmetals share electrons and make a covalent compound.
column29: Find both elements on the periodic table. Are they metals or nonmetals?

column9: Only one of these elements sits right of the staircase. Which one is the nonmetal?
column28: Bromine is right of the staircase, so it is a nonmetal. Iron, barium, and lithium are all left of the staircase, so they are metals.
column29: Nonmetals are on the right side of the staircase line.

column9: Which phrase describes what happens to electrons in an ionic bond?
column14: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another
column15: Electrons are shared between two atoms
column16: Protons are shared between two atoms
column17: Neutrons move from one atom to another
column28: In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred: the metal gives them and the nonmetal takes them. Sharing electrons is a covalent bond. Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus.
column29: Think of the lunch money analogy: one person hands a dollar to another.

column9: Two oxygen atoms bond to make oxygen gas, O₂. What kind of bond holds them together?
column14: Ionic: one oxygen gives electrons to the other
column15: Covalent: the two nonmetal atoms share electrons
column17: No bond: atoms of the same element cannot bond
column28: Oxygen is a nonmetal, and two nonmetals share electrons, so O₂ has a covalent bond (a double bond). Neither oxygen atom is a giver, so no electrons are transferred.
column29: Is there a metal in O₂ to give electrons away?

column9: Sodium (a metal) and chlorine (a nonmetal) join to make table salt, NaCl. A metal + nonmetal compound like this is called a(n) ___ compound.
column28: A metal bonded to a nonmetal makes an ionic compound. The metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal.
column29: Metal + nonmetal = transfer of electrons. Which compound type is that?

column9: By the octet rule, most atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons. The two exceptions are helium and ___.
column28: Hydrogen and helium are the exceptions: they are stable with just 2 outer electrons. Almost every other element is stable with 8.
column29: It is the very first element on the periodic table.

column9: Which group of elements already has a full outer shell, so its atoms almost never form compounds?
column28: Noble gases like neon and argon already have a full outer shell, so they are already stable and have no reason to bond. Groups 1 and 17 bond very easily.
column29: Atoms bond to become stable. Which group is already stable?

column9: Which of these elements is a metal, even though it is not in Group 1 or 2?
column28: Iron is a transition metal, left of the staircase, so it is a metal. Sulfur and carbon are nonmetals, and neon is a noble gas.
column29: Metals are everything left of the staircase, including the transition metals in the middle.

column9: Sugar is a covalent compound. Which property would you expect sugar to have?
column17: It is made of a metal and a nonmetal
column28: Covalent compounds have low melting points and do not conduct when dissolved. Melting above 800 °C and conducting in solution are ionic properties, and a metal + nonmetal would be ionic.
column29: Covalent bonds hold small molecules together. Are they hard or easy to melt?

column9: An atom or group of atoms that has a positive or negative charge is called an ___.
column28: A charged atom or group of atoms is an ion. Metals form positive ions and nonmetals form negative ions, and ionic compounds are made of ions.
column29: It is the first part of the word ionic.

column9: Ana has two white powders. Which test would help her tell which one is ionic?
column14: Dissolve each one and test whether the solution conducts electricity
column17: Check which shelf each one came from
column28: Conductivity when dissolved depends on the bond type: ionic compounds break into free-moving ions and conduct, and covalent ones do not. Color, mass, and storage spot are irrelevant evidence.
column29: Pick the test whose result depends on whether electrons were transferred or shared.

column9: Which of these is a polyatomic ion?
column28: A polyatomic ion is a group of atoms that has a charge together, like nitrate, NO₃⁻ (1 N + 3 O). Cl⁻, Na⁺, and O²⁻ are each a single charged atom.
column29: Poly means many. Which ion is made of more than one atom?

column9: Zinc is a transition metal. What type of compound is zinc chloride, ZnCl₂?
column14: Ionic: zinc is a metal and chlorine is a nonmetal
column15: Covalent: zinc is not in Group 1 or 2
column16: Covalent: zinc and chlorine are both nonmetals
column28: Zinc is left of the staircase, so it is a metal, even though it is not in Group 1 or 2. Metal + nonmetal makes an ionic compound.
column29: Is zinc left or right of the staircase?

column9: Which statement about covalent compounds is true?
column14: They do not conduct electricity when dissolved in water
column28: Covalent compounds stay as whole molecules when they dissolve, so there are no free ions to carry current. They have low melting points, can be solids, liquids, or gases, and contain no metal.
column29: Covalent compounds are made of molecules, not ions. What does that mean for conducting?

column9: Which of these compounds are a metal bonded to a nonmetal (ionic)? Select all that apply.
column28: NaI, MgF₂, and Ca₃N₂ each start with a metal (Na, Mg, Ca), so they are ionic. CS₂, NH₃, and PBr₃ are made only of nonmetals, so they are covalent.
column29: Check the first element of each formula: is it left of the staircase?

column9: Which of these compounds are made only of nonmetals, so they are covalent? Select all that apply.
column28: H₂S, CF₄, and P₄O₁₀ contain only nonmetals, so they are covalent. BaO, K₂S, and AgCl each have a metal (barium, potassium, silver), so they are ionic. Silver is a transition metal.
column29: Covalent means no metal. Remember that hydrogen is a nonmetal and silver is a metal.

column9: Oxygen gas, O₂, has one double bond. How many electrons are shared in a double bond?
column28: A double bond is two shared pairs: 2 × 2 = 4 electrons. A single bond shares 2 and a triple bond shares 6.
column29: Each bond is one shared pair of electrons. How many bonds are in a double bond?

column9: Ionic compounds generally have high melting points, above about 300 °C.
column28: True. Ionic bonds are strong, so ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C. Table salt melts at 801 °C. Covalent compounds melt at much lower temperatures.
column29: Think about how hard it is to melt table salt compared with ice or sugar.

column9: Which substance is most likely ionic?
column14: A white solid that melts at 770 °C
column28: Ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C, so the solid that melts at 770 °C is most likely ionic. The others melt or boil at low temperatures, which points to covalent.
column29: Compare each one to the 300 °C guideline for ionic compounds.

column9: A compound is a gas at room temperature. Is it more likely ionic or covalent?
column14: Covalent, because covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points
column15: Ionic, because ionic compounds are usually gases
column17: Covalent, because it must contain a metal
column28: Ionic compounds are usually solid crystals with high melting points. A gas at room temperature has very low melting and boiling points, which points to covalent. Covalent compounds contain no metal.
column29: Which type of compound can be a solid, liquid, or gas at room temperature?

column9: When an ionic bond forms, which kind of element gives away electrons?
column28: In an ionic bond, the metal gives electrons away and becomes a positive ion; the nonmetal takes them and becomes a negative ion. Sharing happens only in covalent bonds.
column29: Metals are the givers and nonmetals are the takers.

column9: Count the covalent compounds in this list: CH₄, KF, NO, CaBr₂. How many are covalent?
column28: CH₄ and NO are made only of nonmetals, so they are covalent: 2. KF and CaBr₂ each have a metal (K, Ca), so they are ionic.
column29: Mark each formula: metal present (ionic) or only nonmetals (covalent). Count the covalent ones.

column9: Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is the main mineral in limestone (carbonate is CO₃²⁻). What type of compound is it?
column14: Ionic: calcium (a metal) is bonded to the carbonate ion
column15: Covalent: carbon and oxygen are nonmetals
column16: Covalent: it is found in rocks
column28: Calcium is a metal bonded to the polyatomic ion carbonate, so CaCO₃ is ionic. The C and O inside carbonate share electrons, but the compound as a whole is ionic. Where it is found is irrelevant.
column29: Check for a metal first, then for a polyatomic ion.

column9: Which of these is made of molecules (covalently bonded units)?
column28: NH₃ (ammonia) is nitrogen and hydrogen, two nonmetals that share electrons, so it is made of molecules. NaCl, MgO, and K₂S are ionic compounds made of ions.
column29: A molecule forms when nonmetals share electrons. Which formula has no metal?

column9: Which of these elements would be the electron giver (the metal) in an ionic compound? Select all that apply.
column28: Aluminum, lead, and tin are left of the staircase, so they are metals. Phosphorus and iodine are nonmetals, and helium is a noble gas.
column29: Find each element on the periodic table. Left of the staircase = metal.

column9: If a compound dissolves in water, that by itself proves the compound is ionic.
column28: False. Many covalent compounds dissolve too, like sugar and rubbing alcohol. Dissolving is not evidence of bond type; test whether the solution conducts electricity instead.
column29: Does sugar dissolve in water? Is sugar ionic?

column9: Which statement best describes a covalent bond?
column15: A metal gives electrons to a nonmetal
column17: A nonmetal gives electrons to a metal
column28: A covalent bond forms when nonmetal atoms share electrons, like friends splitting a pizza. A metal giving electrons to a nonmetal is an ionic bond.
column29: Covalent = co (together). The atoms use the electrons together.

column9: Solid ionic compounds, like table salt, are usually found as –
column28: Ionic compounds form crystals: the ions stack in a repeating pattern. They have high melting points, so they are solids at room temperature, and they are made of ions, not molecules.
column29: Look closely at grains of table salt. What shape are they?

column9: Kayla tests four unknowns. Which result points most strongly to an ionic compound?
column14: Melts at 850 °C, and its solution conducts electricity
column15: Melts at 60 °C, and its solution does not conduct
column16: Forms white crystals and feels heavy
column17: Is bright blue and dissolves in water
column28: Both observations in the key are relevant and both point to ionic: a melting point far above 300 °C and free ions in solution. Color, mass, crystals, and dissolving do not decide bond type.
column29: Use the two tests that depend on bond type: melting point and conductivity.

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻, ammonium is NH₄⁺, and sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Which of these compounds are ionic? Select all that apply.
column28: KOH (metal + hydroxide), NH₄I (ammonium), and MgSO₄ (metal + sulfate) are ionic. N₂O₄, H₂O, and CH₄ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, so they are covalent.
column29: A compound is ionic if it has a metal OR a polyatomic ion. Check each formula for both.

column9: Which pair of elements would NOT form a compound by transferring electrons?
column28: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons (covalent) instead of transferring them. Each other pair is a metal with a nonmetal, which transfers electrons (ionic).
column29: Electrons are transferred only when a metal meets a nonmetal. Which pair has no metal?

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺. Which compound is ionic?
column28: NH₄F contains the polyatomic ion ammonium, so it is ionic even though it has no metal. SF₆, N₂O₅, and CCl₄ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, so they are covalent.
column29: None of these has a metal. Look for a polyatomic ion instead.

column9: Ty says lead(II) oxide, PbO, is covalent because lead is close to the staircase and not in Group 1 or 2. Which response is best?
column14: Ty is wrong: lead is left of the staircase, so it is a metal, and PbO is ionic
column15: Ty is right: only Group 1 and 2 elements are metals
column16: Ty is right: oxygen always makes a compound covalent
column17: Ty is wrong: PbO is ionic because oxygen is a metal
column28: Lead sits left of the staircase, so it is a metal, and a metal + nonmetal compound is ionic. Metals are not only in Groups 1 and 2, and oxygen is a nonmetal.
column29: Find lead (Pb) on the periodic table. Which side of the staircase is it on?

column9: Match each molecule to the total number of electrons shared in all of its bonds.
column28: Single bond = 2, double = 4, triple = 6. H–F: one single = 2. O=O: one double = 4. H–O–O–H: three singles = 6. H–C≡N: one single + one triple = 2 + 6 = 8.
column29: Count each line in the drawing. One line shares 2 electrons, two lines share 4, and three lines share 6.

column9: Group 1 metals bond with Group 17 nonmetals (like K with Cl). What kind of compounds do they form?
column14: Ionic: the metal transfers an electron to the nonmetal
column16: Ionic: the nonmetal transfers electrons to the metal
column17: None: both groups are already stable
column28: Group 1 elements are metals and Group 17 elements are nonmetals, so they form ionic compounds: the metal gives its electron to the nonmetal. Neither group is already stable (that is Group 18).
column29: Which group is the giver, and which is the taker?

column9: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons. How does it become stable when it bonds with sodium?
column15: It loses all 7 of its outer electrons
column28: Most atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons. Chlorine needs just 1 more, so it takes 1 electron from sodium (a metal) and becomes Cl⁻. That transfer is an ionic bond.
column29: How many more electrons does chlorine need to reach 8?

column9: An unknown melts at 1,100 °C, its solution conducts electricity, and it is green. Which conclusion and evidence are best?
column14: Ionic, because of the high melting point and the conductivity
column15: Ionic, because of the green color
column16: Covalent, because of the high melting point
column17: Covalent, because conducting means electrons are shared
column28: A melting point far above 300 °C and a conducting solution both point to ionic. Color is irrelevant evidence, and conducting in solution comes from free ions, not shared electrons.
column29: Ignore any evidence that does not depend on bond type.

column9: Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄, is a covalent compound once used in fire extinguishers. Which of these describe CCl₄? Select all that apply.
column15: It has a low melting point
column28: CCl₄ is covalent: it has a low melting point, its atoms share electrons, and it is made of molecules. Melting above 300 °C and conducting in solution are ionic properties.
column29: Recall the properties of covalent compounds, then check each statement.

column9: Four unknowns are tested. W: melts at 993 °C; its solution conducts. X: melts at 44 °C; its solution does not conduct. Y: melts at 604 °C; its solution conducts. Z: melts at −23 °C (a liquid at room temperature); it does not conduct. Select every unknown that is most likely covalent. Select all that apply.
column28: X and Z melt far below 300 °C and do not conduct, so they are covalent. W and Y melt well above 300 °C and conduct when dissolved, so they are ionic.
column29: Sort with both tests: melting point (about 300 °C) and conductivity.

column9: Ben says copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄, must be covalent because it has more nonmetal atoms (S and O) than metal atoms. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Which response is best?
column14: Ben is wrong: copper is a metal bonded to the polyatomic ion sulfate, so CuSO₄ is ionic; counting atoms does not decide
column15: Ben is right: more nonmetal atoms always means covalent
column16: Ben is right: the S and O inside sulfate share electrons, so the compound is covalent
column17: Ben is wrong: CuSO₄ is ionic because sulfur is a metal
column28: Copper is a metal (a transition metal), and sulfate is a polyatomic ion, so CuSO₄ is ionic. The S and O inside sulfate do share electrons, but a metal + polyatomic ion compound is classified as ionic. Sulfur is a nonmetal.
column29: Check for a metal and a polyatomic ion. Does the number of each kind of atom matter?

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻. Sort this list: LiCl, NH₄NO₃, CS₂, Fe(NO₃)₃, SO₂, BaO, NCl₃. How many of these compounds are covalent?
column28: Covalent (only nonmetals, no polyatomic ion): CS₂, SO₂, and NCl₃ = 3. Ionic: LiCl and BaO (metal + nonmetal), Fe(NO₃)₃ (metal + nitrate), and NH₄NO₃ (two polyatomic ions, no metal needed).
column29: A compound is covalent only if it has no metal AND no polyatomic ion.

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺. Mia sorted compounds into piles labeled "covalent." Which pile has no mistakes?
column28: CO₂, NH₃, and PCl₅ are all only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion. Each other pile hides an ionic compound: NaCl (metal), NH₄Cl (ammonium ion), and CuO (copper is a metal).
column29: In each pile, hunt for a metal or a polyatomic ion. One of them would make that compound ionic.

column9: Ethane, H₃C–CH₃, has 7 single bonds. Ethene, H₂C=CH₂, has 1 double bond and 4 single bonds. How many more electrons are shared in ethane than in ethene?
column28: Ethane: 7 single bonds × 2 = 14 electrons. Ethene: one double bond (4) + four single bonds (4 × 2 = 8) = 12 electrons. Difference: 14 − 12 = 2.
column29: Find the total shared electrons in each molecule (single = 2, double = 4), then subtract.

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻ and acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. A student must circle every ionic compound in this list. Which should be circled? Select all that apply.
column28: Mn(OH)₂ (metal + hydroxide), NaC₂H₃O₂ (metal + acetate), and NiO (nickel is a metal) are ionic. C₂H₆, H₂O₂, and OF₂ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, even though C₂H₆ and H₂O₂ contain some of the same letters as acetate and hydroxide.
column29: Look for a metal symbol first. A formula made only of C, H, O, or F with no metal and no listed ion is covalent.

column9: KCl and HCl both have a Group 1 element bonded to chlorine. Which statement about their bonds is correct?
column14: In KCl, potassium transfers an electron to chlorine (ionic); in HCl, hydrogen and chlorine share electrons (covalent)
column15: Both are ionic, because both contain chlorine
column16: Both are ionic, because K and H are both in Group 1
column17: KCl is covalent and HCl is ionic
column28: Potassium is a metal, so KCl is ionic (transfer). Hydrogen sits in Group 1 but is a nonmetal, so HCl is two nonmetals sharing electrons (covalent).
column29: Is hydrogen a metal or a nonmetal? Classify each compound separately.

column9: Four groups each tested an unknown and made a claim. Which claim is supported by relevant evidence?
column14: "Ionic: it melts at 950 °C and its solution conducts."
column28: Only the first claim uses relevant evidence that fits: a high melting point and a conducting solution both point to ionic. Shininess, mass, and color are irrelevant, and a 900 °C melting point points to ionic, not covalent.
column29: A good claim needs evidence that depends on bond type AND points the same way as the claim.

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column14: In NaCl, sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
column15: In H₂O, oxygen takes electrons away from hydrogen
column16: In Cl₂, the two chlorine atoms share electrons
column17: In CaO, calcium and oxygen share electrons
column18: In N₂, one nitrogen atom transfers electrons to the other
column19: In NH₄Cl, the ammonium ion plays the part of the metal ion
column28: True: NaCl is metal + nonmetal (transfer); Cl₂ is two nonmetals (sharing); in NH₄Cl, ammonium acts like the metal ion. False: H₂O and N₂ are nonmetals that share, and CaO is metal + nonmetal, so electrons are transferred, not shared.
column29: Classify each compound first: metal + nonmetal or polyatomic ion = transfer (ionic); only nonmetals = sharing (covalent).

column9: Which compound breaks apart into free-moving ions when it dissolves in water?
column28: KNO₃ is ionic: a metal (potassium) with the polyatomic ion nitrate, so it splits into K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions and conducts. Glucose, methanol, and ethanol are covalent, so they stay as whole molecules.
column29: Only ionic compounds break into ions. Which formula has a metal or a polyatomic ion?
